title: The Day Indian Cricket Hit Rock Bottom — Twice
excerpt: Ireland completed a historic 2-0 T20I sweep in Belfast while Australia ended India's Women's T20 World Cup campaign at Lord's, all within hours of each other. For the diaspora, Sunday was a painful double bill.
body:
Sunday, June 28, 2026, will not be remembered fondly in Indian cricketing circles. In the span of a few brutal hours, the men's team completed a historic capitulation in Belfast — swept 2-0 by Ireland in a bilateral T20I series — while the women's squad saw their T20 World Cup campaign end at Lord's, falling agonisingly short against Australia.

For the Indian diaspora scattered across time zones, it was a rare and painful double bill. Two matches. Two defeats. Two different continents. One shared sense of disbelief.

## Belfast: How Ireland Made History — Again

Three days after handing India their first-ever T20I defeat to Ireland, the hosts proved it was no fluke. Ireland restricted India to 153/9 chasing 155, securing a one-run victory that completed a 2-0 series sweep — the first time any team has blanked India in a bilateral T20I series since Sri Lanka in 2023.

Player-of-the-series Jai Moondra — the Rajasthan-born seamer who qualifies for Ireland through residency — was devastating again, dismissing both Indian openers in his very first over. Sanju Samson fell for a golden duck for the second consecutive match, a statistic that will haunt him. Shreyas Iyer, the captain, was bowled by Moondra in the third over, leaving India reeling at 19/3.

Tilak Varma's fighting 55 kept India in the hunt, and Harshit Rana's late blitz (21 off 10 balls) brought the equation down to eight runs from the final two deliveries. But Rana was caught on the boundary trying to clear Harry Tector off the penultimate ball. Game over. Series over.

"Kudos to them, the way they played. They showed professionalism," a visibly dejected Iyer conceded at the post-match presentation.

Ireland captain Lorcan Tucker was more direct: "I challenged the lads the other day to show the world that wasn't a one-off. We have a lot of lads with very few caps but they showed great character."

## Lord's: Two Runs Short, and a World Cup Over

Across the Irish Sea at Lord's, the stakes were existential. India needed to beat Australia to stay alive in the Women's T20 World Cup — and Harmanpreet Kaur's side came within two runs of doing exactly that.

Batting first after winning the toss, India posted 170/4, a competitive total anchored by Smriti Mandhana and a characteristically combative knock from Harmanpreet. Deepti Sharma, in a historic personal milestone, surpassed Jhulan Goswami's all-time record to become the highest wicket-taker in women's T20I history with her 356th scalp.

But Australia, propelled by Ellyse Perry and Ashleigh Gardner, chased down the target with four wickets in hand, reaching 172/4 with seven balls to spare. It was clinical, ruthless, and quintessentially Australian.

India's elimination means South Africa advance to the semifinals alongside Australia from Group A. For a team that has now failed to reach the last four in the past two T20 World Cups, the questions are mounting.

## What Went Wrong — and What Comes Next

The twin defeats expose familiar vulnerabilities. The men's top order remains fragile when conditions don't suit strokeplay — Samson's two golden ducks in two matches, Abhishek Sharma's inability to convert starts, and Iyer's struggles against pace are patterns, not aberrations. The decision to rest frontline stars like Jasprit Bumrah and Suryakumar Yadav for the Ireland tour has backfired spectacularly. A second-string squad was meant to gain experience; instead, it gifted Ireland a lifetime of cricketing memories.

The women's team has a different problem: consistency against the top sides. India beat Pakistan and competed hard against England, but when the tournament's decisive match arrived, they couldn't close it out. The gap between India and the established powers — Australia, England, South Africa — remains stubbornly wide.

## The Diaspora Watches, and Winces

For NRIs waking up to Sunday morning cricket in the US, the mood was grim. Social media erupted with frustration, memes, and the kind of gallows humour that only cricket fans can produce. "My dad's anger at breakfast suddenly made sense — he'd been checking both scores on his phone," one fan wrote on an Indian forum.

The timing stung particularly hard. The men's team heads to England in three days for a five-match T20I series starting July 1, followed by three ODIs where Virat Kohli makes his return. There is no time to lick wounds. The selectors face immediate decisions: does Samson keep his place after consecutive golden ducks? Should Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, the 15-year-old prodigy left out of the Ireland squad, be fast-tracked into the England XI? Can Iyer justify the captaincy after being outplayed by a team ranked twelfth in the world?

The women's team, meanwhile, heads home with time to reflect. Harmanpreet has already spoken about her ambition to lead the side at the LA 2028 Olympics, where cricket will feature for the first time since 1900. But the road from Lord's heartbreak to Olympic glory is long, and the competition is not getting any easier.

## One Day, Two Lessons

Irish cricket celebrated the greatest day in its history. Australian women's cricket confirmed its supremacy once more. And Indian cricket — men's and women's — was left searching for answers on the same painful Sunday.

The talent is there. The depth, increasingly, is there. But on June 28, 2026, none of it was enough.

*India's men play their first T20I against England at Edgbaston on July 1. The Women's T20 World Cup semifinals are scheduled for July 3 at The Oval.*
